name: Mean, Total, and Number of Observations
description: Connect the arithmetic mean to the total and the number of observations. Learn to interpret units, estimate a sensible result, and check whether an average must be an observed value.
script_scope: Define the arithmetic mean as total sum divided by number of observations, and derive the equivalent total = mean × count. Explain that an average is a balance point, may be fractional or absent from the data, and uses the same units as the observations. Teach reliable summation, unit consistency, rounding only at the end, and bounds/sanity checks. Include simple lists, marks, weights, and money examples at the chapter's level. Learners should compute a mean, recover a total from a mean and count, and explain what the result says and does not say.

name: Missing Values and Reverse-Average Equations
description: Recover an unknown observation from a group mean, or use multiple averages to solve for missing values.
script_scope: Use total = mean × count to turn an average statement into an equation. Subtract known observations from the required total to find one missing value; handle two linked averages by solving equations in sequence. Cover an unknown added to a set, one unknown in two overlapping groups, and relationships among unknown values when supported by the chapter. Show how to check by restoring the total and recomputing the mean. Learners should distinguish a missing observation from a missing group count and reject results that violate stated constraints.

name: Averages of Consecutive and Patterned Sets
description: Use symmetry and sequence structure to find means of consecutive numbers, multiples, and regular lists efficiently.
script_scope: Teach the midpoint property for equally spaced lists: for a finite arithmetic progression, the mean is the average of the first and last terms because pairs equidistant from the ends share the same midpoint. Derive rather than merely state the property. Apply it to consecutive integers, odd/even numbers, multiples, and a specified finite set such as primes by summing actual terms when the spacing is irregular. Include first n natural numbers and first n multiples using the chapter's sum formula, and carefully interpret endpoints such as strictly between. Learners should choose between pairing, a sequence formula, and direct summation, then verify term count and boundaries.

name: Weighted and Combined Averages
description: Combine subgroup averages using their sizes so each observation contributes the right amount.
script_scope: Derive the combined mean as (n₁a₁+n₂a₂+…)/(n₁+n₂+…), where each subgroup mean is weighted by its observation count. Explain why averaging subgroup means directly is valid only when group sizes are equal. Apply to boys/girls, sections, workers, time periods, prices, and other chapter-supported grouped data. Convert group means to totals before combining; keep units consistent and distinguish counts from averages. Learners should calculate a weighted mean, infer a missing group mean or count when sufficient information exists, and check that the combined value lies between subgroup means.

name: Overlapping Groups and Shared Observations
description: Use group totals to handle overlapping lists, shared members, and averages of first and last sections.
script_scope: Translate each group average into its group total, then account for members included in both groups exactly once. Teach the overlap identity: total(A)+total(B)=total(union)+total(intersection), and its use for a missing shared observation or middle value. Cover first/last overlapping subsets, pairwise sums for three people, and inclusive group counting as shown in the chapter. Label counts and shared members before calculating; explain why subtracting an overlap is necessary. Learners should draw or list group membership, avoid double-counting, solve the unknown, and verify each stated group total.

name: Changing Averages: Additions, Departures, and Replacements
description: Track how a group total changes when members join, leave, or are replaced, and infer the missing contribution.
script_scope: Model a group's total before and after a membership change using mean × count. Derive the total increase/decrease from the difference in averages, then isolate the contribution of a person or incoming/outgoing group. Cover a single person joining or leaving, a teacher or student added, and one or more replacements; keep the count correct at every stage. Use consistent units (for example, convert 100 g to 0.1 kg or months to years) and check by reconstructing both group totals. Learners should distinguish change in average from change in total and avoid multiplying by the wrong group size.

name: Averages Across Ages, Marks, and Time
description: Solve average-age and performance problems by tracking totals as time passes or scores are added and removed.
script_scope: Apply the mean-total-count model to ages, class marks, innings, and repeated tests. Explain that when all k people remain in a group, each person's age rises by t over t years, so the group total rises by kt and the average rises by t; membership changes require separate total accounting. Cover a score changing a running average, excluding high/low observations, adding births or entrants, and time-unit conversions (months to years). Learners should set a clear time reference, calculate totals at that time, respect integer/count constraints, and check the resulting ages or scores in the original scenario.

name: Average Speed for Equal-Distance Journeys
description: Find overall speed from distance and time, especially when a journey has equal distances at different speeds.
script_scope: Define average speed as total distance divided by total time. For equal distances d at speeds x and y, derive total time d/x+d/y and simplify the average speed to 2xy/(x+y), the harmonic mean. Explain why the ordinary arithmetic mean of the speeds is wrong for equal-distance legs, while equal-time legs do use the arithmetic mean of the speeds. Work units consistently and use a magnitude check: the overall speed must lie between the two leg speeds and is closer to the slower speed for equal distances. Learners should identify what is equal, choose the correct formula, and verify using distance/time.

name: Ratios, Bounds, and Constraints on an Average
description: Use average relationships to infer ratios, test possible values, and reason about bounds and percentage changes.
script_scope: Translate average information into equations alongside ratios or inequalities. Cover subgroup ratio weighting, consecutive-value constraints, positive integer conditions, averages of nonnegative or signed observations, and basic maximum/minimum reasoning supported by the chapter. Explain that a mean lies between the minimum and maximum observations, but endpoint inclusion and integrality can narrow possibilities. Include percentage change in an average or rate only when the base value and units are explicit. Learners should identify whether the data determine a unique answer, use bounds to reject impossible options, and avoid treating an average as an individual observation.

name: Integrated Average Problems and Data Sufficiency
description: Choose and combine average methods in multi-step problems, including deciding whether information is sufficient to determine an answer.
script_scope: Consolidate the chapter with fresh multi-step problems that combine at least two skills: weighted means with a missing group size, membership changes followed by a new mean, overlapping subsets, ages across time, or a speed problem requiring total distance and time. Include data-sufficiency reasoning at the source's level: test each statement alone and in combination, distinguish a unique answer from merely possible answers, and do not calculate beyond what is asked. Teach a solve plan that defines counts and units, converts means to totals, chooses a valid relationship, checks constraints, and verifies by substitution or bounds. Do not extract or reproduce the book's objective questions.
